papers.abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.
authors: Haolin Jiang, Weihang Li, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jinwen Pan, Santosh Pandey, Hang Liu
bullets: Linear-attention queries, keys, and values concentrate in a stable low-dimensional subspace, making recurrent states effectively low-rank.
Dense state updates create substantial memory traffic that grows with batch size and can dominate decoding cost.
SinkState uses buffered updates, local SVD over the top subspace, and asynchronous CPU consolidation.
Across four hybrid models using Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet layers, it reduces recurrent-state peak memory by up to 2.6× and speeds decoding by up to 1.58× while maintaining accuracy.

papers.abstract: Establishing dense correspondence between high-resolution 3D shapes remains challenging due to the spatial--spectral coupling at the core of many functional-map methods, which grows quadratically with mesh resolution. We observe that this coupling is equivalent to a scaled dot-product attention formulation, with learned descriptors serving as queries and keys and spectral basis functions as values. This connection makes efficient attention implementations directly applicable to shape matching and an effective mechanism for scaling spatial-spectral coupling. We show that optimized quadratic attention implementations can scale modern deep functional map pipelines to large mesh sizes, improving both runtime and memory consumption, while sub-quadratic methods introduce errors, particularly for non-isometric shape pairs, where an exact coupling proves most necessary. These insights motivate \textit{Geo-FlashAttention}, which restricts the exact softmax to geometry-selected surface patches and achieves near-linear empirical scaling while preserving correspondence accuracy of exact implementations. Across six standard benchmarks and three functional-map pipelines, rigorous analysis shows that efficient couplings preserve correspondence accuracy. At $60k$ vertices, these insights reduce peak training memory from 106.08 to 5.67\,GiB, with Geo-FlashAttention being $1.5\times$ faster per training step than FlashAttention. This enables end-to-end learning for correspondence problems on large meshes such as cortical surfaces, where high resolution is required to preserve disease-relevant intricacies of the surface geometry. Project page available https://spatial-spectral-attention.github.io/
authors: Bence Demeter, Kilian Ehrenreich, Amelie Kleber, Ioana Oprisiu, Philipp Spohn, Christian Wachinger, Fabian Bongratz, Lennart Bastian
bullets: Functional-map coupling scales quadratically with mesh resolution, limiting dense correspondence on large surfaces.
The paper identifies this coupling with scaled dot-product attention, enabling optimized attention implementations for shape matching.
Sub-quadratic approximations can introduce errors, especially for non-isometric shape pairs requiring exact coupling.
Geo-FlashAttention applies exact softmax attention only to geometry-selected surface patches.

Across six benchmarks and three pipelines, efficient couplings preserve accuracy; at 60k vertices, memory drops from 106.08 to 5.67 GiB, and Geo-FlashAttention is 1.5× faster per step than FlashAttention.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of Geo-FlashAttention. (1) Target N and source M are partitioned into geometrically derived patches A and B based on vertex positions. (2) Each source patch Br is summarised by its mean key µr . (3) Target queries are scored against the pooled keys and reduced per patch pair by sar = maxi∈Aa q⊤i µr . (4) The R best-scoring source patches per target patch form the support Sa,R, so every row keeps exactly R patches. (5) A fused block-sparse kernel evaluates the exact softmax without materialising Π̃ (R) NM .

Figure 1. Scalability challenges of Deep Spectral Methods. Spectral matching methods often rely on recovering a point-topoint map ΠNM , either to convert a functional map back to the spatial domain or as an effective regularization. Comparing shape vertex features requires O(nM · nN ) operations, which is infeasible with current strategies.

Figure 4. Comparing attention computations. (1) Dense softmax forms the full nN × nM correspondence matrix, while FlashAttention (2) tiles A through on-chip memory. (3) Linear attention replaces the softmax kernel by a feature map φ approximating the product. (4) Geo-FlashAttention evaluates exact softmax attention on the induced vertex support by S.

papers.abstract: Music editing transforms existing recordings while preserving their original attributes. Recent approaches adapt pretrained text-to-music models for tasks like inpainting, event insertion, or restoration by conditioning them with context audio. It was recently proposed for image editing to unify generation and editing by treating the source image as in-context information. However, applying this directly to music is computationally expensive due to long audio sequences. In this work, we develop MusicFlux, a text-guided music editor built on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model. We introduce two conditioning approaches that trade off editing performance and computational efficiency. Experiments show that both are competitive with strong baselines, with one achieving better editing quality and the other preserving the original sequence length and substantially improving computational efficiency.

bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of adapting text-to-music models for editing long audio sequences.
Introduces two conditioning strategies that trade off editing quality and computational efficiency.
Both strategies are competitive with strong baselines.
One improves editing quality, while the other preserves original sequence length and substantially increases efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.
authors: Haoyi Wu, Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang, Lei Wang, Wenbin Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of defending against jailbreaks without predefined safety directions or excessive over-refusal.
Calibrates attention entropy against each prompt’s prefill baseline, then uses scale normalization and temporal accumulation to estimate intervention strength.
Applies bounded modulation to the model’s own residual updates, avoiding predefined representational targets.
Evaluated against seven defenses across seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks on Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models.
Reports improved jailbreak robustness, low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests, and modest inference overhead.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

papers.title: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
authors: Dayou Du, Woon Yee Ng, Guangming Sheng, Nick Lau, Jianyi Cheng, Luo Mai
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Uses dual-residual query quantization, underflow-aware probability scaling, and outlier-aware key quantization to reduce FP4 accuracy loss.
Removes softmax overhead with transposed softmax, fused probability quantization, and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches.
Stays within 0.5 accuracy points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 and within 1 point with MXFP4 across dense and MoE models.
On NVIDIA B300, achieves 2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV for Qwen3 models.

papers.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design

papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
bullets: Targets decode attention, where quantized KV caches reduce memory traffic but can remain latency-bound by dequantization overhead.
Uses affine folding tailored to token-wise or channel-wise quantization, preserving the exact dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic.
Employs bit manipulation and warp-specialized Hopper/Blackwell GPU pipelines to efficiently feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores.
Reports substantial kernel speedups on H100 and B200 against BF16, FP8, and, in some cases, NVFP4 baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves peak aggregate throughput on long-context serving workloads by up to 170% versus 2-bit and 341% versus 16-bit baselines.

papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
bullets: Targets the computational and KV-memory bottleneck of attention as context length grows.
Uses each head’s query-key operator to determine an effective feature rank and compact response space.
Merges neighboring token regions when their responses are directionally coherent, while preserving heterogeneous regions separately.
Computes exact attention with original full-dimensional KV states for selected regions.
Captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass, improves reported RULER and LongBench-Pro accuracy over UNIQUE by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points, and reaches up to 14.07× speedup over dense attention.

papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
authors: Tianxing Wu, Juuso Korhonen, Jesus Carabano Bravo
bullets: Addresses softmax as the bottleneck preventing attention from exploiting rapidly increasing low-precision matrix throughput.
Introduces a training-free approximation that folds dominant softmax operations into attention GEMMs.
On AMD CDNA 4, MXFP8/6/4 kernels achieve about 3.0/4.0/4.6 PFLOP/s and 2.1×/2.8×/3.2× speedups over BF16 attention.
A hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule provides up to 2.05× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B without degrading visual quality.
Implemented in AMD’s open-source AITER library and used in an MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
authors: Jo\~ao Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, Mohamed Wahib
bullets: Targets full-attention layers that remain costly at long contexts in hybrid models.

Across six models and 21 long-context datasets, configurations preserve baseline accuracy.
Provides up to 2.22× faster decoding at 256k tokens, depending on the model.

papers.abstract: High-content multi-channel imaging, from Cell Painting assays to remote sensing, is central to modern scientific pipelines. Because these channels are highly heterogeneous and experimental configurations frequently evolve, a practical vision backbone must be fundamentally channel-agnostic. Current channel-adaptive vision transformers rely on global self-attention with learnable channel embeddings, which can be computed only for previously known channels. Attempts to overcome this limitation of new channels either discard the embeddings, losing channel identity, or process each channel independently, thereby eliminating critical cross-channel interactions. To address this, we introduce ChanSFormer, an efficient Vision Transformer that replaces rigid embeddings with disentangled spatial-channel attention and individual channel CLS tokens. This architecture natively preserves both distinct channel identities and cross-channel information flow. Furthermore, the individual channel class token design unlocks more informative feature representations for self-supervised learning and enables representation-based channel sampling while remaining channel-agnostic. We evaluate ChanSFormer on two biology multi-channel datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP and a satellite dataset, So2Sat. Experimental results show that ChanSFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.93%-4.27% on JUMP-CP in classification accuracy. It also demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset transferability under a self-supervised setting, outperforming previous methods by up to 2.72% in accuracy in the same classification tasks. Furthermore, the disentangled attention reduces the quadratic complexity of channel-by-spatial sequence length of the global attention baseline, thus improving throughput by 55%-313%. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/ChanSFormer.
authors: Jingwei Zhang, Srinivasan Sivanandan, Dimitris Samaras
bullets: Addresses the limitation of channel-adaptive transformers that depend on predefined channel embeddings and handle new channels poorly.
Uses disentangled spatial-channel attention with individual channel CLS tokens to retain channel identities and enable cross-channel information flow.
Supports more informative self-supervised representations and representation-based channel sampling.
Evaluated on CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat; on JUMP-CP, it improves classification accuracy by 3.93–4.27% over state-of-the-art methods and improves cross-dataset transfer by up to 2.72%.
Reduces attention complexity and improves throughput by 55–313% compared with global attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang
bullets: Targets identification overhead, poor uniform/local budget allocation, and stale masks or clusters in sparse video diffusion attention.
Uses semantic clusters to compensate skipped keys and exact attention on a small set of offline-fixed blocks to correct residual error.
Introduces Distortion Budget to allocate exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads based on its effect on final-latent distortion.
Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.title: DecoupAttn: Decoupled Sparse Attention for Training-Free Acceleration of Video Diffusion

papers.abstract: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.
authors: Xinhang Zhang, Boning Zhang, Chengchun Liu, Chunpu Li, Lei Sun, Weifeng Zhang, Limin Xiao
bullets: Targets poor GPU utilization from communication dependencies in sequence-parallel attention, especially under cross-hardware bandwidth imbalance.
Uses hierarchical sequential communication to enable intra-level parallelism and overlap communication with computation.
Decouples cross-hardware and intra-hardware communication to remove synchronization overhead caused by unequal bandwidth.
Evaluated forward and backward attention across multiple hardware architectures, outperforming prior methods.
Against Ring-Attention, reports 1.3×/1.7× average forward/backward speedups on dual-NUMA PCIe and 2.8×/2.9× on dual-node NVLink.

(b) shows the parallel communication and computation of q and kv. In this step, GPU 3 communicates q with GPU 0 and kv with GPU 1. After completing the computation of Q0,4, GPU3 communicates back to GPU 0 and receives the output. (c) performs the last step of RM+, where GPU 3 only communicates kv with GPU 2. (d) shows that once all kv results are computed, the output is communicated back to GPU 7. (e) illustrates the overall cross-NUMA communication and the full overlap of computation and communication of GPU3 happened in (a)-(d).

papers.abstract: Expert offloading enables large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models to run locally, but conventional batching stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. A popular remedy, known as prefetching, is to predict what experts will be needed soon and fetch them using idle link bandwidth. Imprecise prediction, however, wastes bandwidth and GPU memory on fetching unnecessary experts. Our key finding is that prefetching can be harmful when there is an expert cache in GPU memory. This is because as the cache includes more necessary experts, expert prediction becomes less precise. Our key insight is that proper request scheduling beats prefetching. Building on this insight, we present Bevy, an MoE inference system based on runahead inference for concurrent requests. A request whose experts are available can run ahead to later layers while other requests wait for fetches, revealing the experts it needs next. Bevy can then fetch the missing experts so identified while computing ready requests, overlapping computation and fetching without predicting expert selections. Running requests separately, however, repeats reads of shared weights in GPU memory and increases compute time. To limit this cost, Bevy's self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes lagging requests, adapting their grouping as expert availability changes. Across two local platforms, Bevy delivers up to 3.46$\times$ the decode throughput of llama.cpp and up to 1.55$\times$ that of the fastest prefetching baseline.
authors: Hongseung Yu, In Gim, Kyunghan Lee, Lin Zhong
bullets: Expert offloading can stall GPU execution when required experts must be fetched.
Prefetching may waste bandwidth and GPU memory because larger expert caches reduce prediction precision.
Bevy uses runahead inference: requests with available experts advance to reveal future needs while others wait.
A self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests and prioritizes lagging requests to reduce repeated weight reads and computation.
Across two local platforms, Bevy achieves up to 3.46× the decode throughput of llama.cpp and 1.55× that of the fastest prefetching baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Bevy, a system for accelerating MoE inference by interleaving concurrent requests and using a self-balancing scheduler. This addresses inference efficiency and optimization, fitting the Efficient AI subtopic.
papers.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
papers.tldr: Bevy accelerates local MoE inference by scheduling concurrent requests to overlap expert fetching with computation, avoiding inaccurate prefetch predictions.

papers.abstract: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/AttentionWithBias.
authors: Charles Herr, Gabriele Spadaro, Enzo Tartaglione
bullets: Attention-matrix columns contribute unequally to the final computation, with this imbalance increasing at greater network depth.
The method adds an input-dependent bias to query–key dot products to estimate each token’s anticipated influence on others.
These scalar token scores act as a proxy for pruning attention maps.
Across multiple transformer sizes, pruning substantially reduces attention FLOPs and inference latency while retaining most classification accuracy.
Code and models are publicly released.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary. Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Michel Barlaud, Clement Genninasca, Maxime Zanella, Benoit Macq, Benoit Legat
bullets: Defines the scale-invariant Cone Alignment Index (CAI) and analyzes its distribution under general, Gaussian, and uniform settings.
Proposes PLCP, a closed-form conic projection approximation, alongside PECP, the exact Euclidean projection.
Proves PLCP and PECP are collinear, preserve the same sparsity threshold, and identify identical active supports.
Establishes theoretical control over the number of coefficients discarded for a target sparsity level.
Extends PLCP to bilevel matrix sparsification with row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal structured masks.

papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes sparse attention and long-context LLM decode, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context model developments.
papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) hides DeepSeek Sparse Attention’s expensive indexer scans by reusing the previous layer’s token selection, delivering faster long-context decoding without retraining.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.tldr: Domain-specific transformer inductive biases can improve language-model training efficiency or generalization, but their benefits often do not transfer across domains.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.
Organizes keys into a learned latent hierarchy, allowing queries to score clusters rather than all keys.
Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.
N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy and provides per-layer training speedups at 128k tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Subquadratic sparse attention for ultra-long context via latent hierarchical key selection; directly fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.tldr: Latent Sparse Attention enables efficient ultra-long-context attention by hierarchically routing queries to learned key clusters instead of examining every key.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Figure 8: For a fixed top-p, and hence sparsity level, ZHA (here, R = 1, C = 8, p = 0.75) scales subquadratically according to our decode roofline model, eventually dramatically outperforming both dense attention and the MSA sparse attention variant. Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

Figure 7: Per-level selection scales sublinearly in the ZHA router with predictable power-law exponent. (a)–(e): For ZHA geometries with depths L = 2–6 (C = 4, R = 16, p = 0.8), per-level selection counts (normalized by first-bin count per-level) on AIME problems fitted by power-law scaling curves. (f): Per-level exponents fitted by cumulative top-down model, demonstrating that the across-depth variation in their exponents is well-described by a simple model that accumulates top-down contributions.

Figure 24: Modeled BF16 decode latency for dense attention, MSA, and ZHA (R = 1, C = 8) at p = 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, with the H100 assumptions and nondecreasing latency-minimizing depth of Figure 8. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

Appendix B gives evaluation details and results across routing thresholds. We observe that ZHA with both wide and deep geometries maintains performance even at high sparsity levels, while MSA suffers performance degradation especially on retrieval tasks such as RULER and LongBench v2.

Greater sparsity without degrading performance is achieved by: (a) decreasing compression CL, (b) increasing depth at fixed compression (CL = 4096), or (c) making key summaries more expressive (with increasing reference-query number R) at fixed chunk size and depth. (The horizontal dotted lines in panels (a)–(c) show dense attention.) (d) For the simple geometry-to-performance model, predictions versus measurements across 64K, 128K, and 256K, holding out each length in turn (RMSE: 1.44 percentage points).

Figure 4: Illustrative ZHA tree geometries of the three core tree parameters. We can trade off depth and width for a given level of compression in the tree, since compression scales as CL. Secondly, at the cost of additional compute, we can increase the number of reference queries.

We observe that for the higher p values we use in practice, a substantial fraction of the total KV cache is included in the union of the queries.

Figure 10: (a) Cosine similarity distribution of every pair of reference queries within a KV group; (b) norm distribution of every reference query. Reference queries within a KV group become slightly more similar and their norms more concentrated as the tree gets shallower and its chunks larger.

(a) Within each KV group and level, reference queries are independently ranked by selection frequency. Each point shows the level’s share of selections at that rank, averaged over layers and KV groups. Higher levels concentrate selections among fewer reference queries, while lower levels use them more uniformly. (b) Spearman correlation between levels’ selection rates. Higher levels have strongly aligned reference-query rankings. Agreement generally weakens as levels become further separated, with the chunk level showing the greatest divergence from the upper levels.

Colours distinguish d ∈ {64, 128, 256}. Dots show all recorded timing samples and short ticks mark medians; solid lines in the latency views show worker-aware predictions. papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang
bullets: Finite-state memory and initialization can limit long-context retrieval in linear attention.
DAMI jointly configures gate parameters before training using geometric head-wise timescales and a low-high-low layer-wise sensitivity profile.
A small activation sample calibrates the implementation to these targets without adding trainable parameters.
Across five gated linear-attention families, DAMI raises average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29–16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
Language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval performance remains broadly comparable to baseline initialization.

papers.abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
bullets: Addresses Transformer KV-cache growth and the limited addressability of fixed-state State Space Models.
Uses multiple complex-diagonal dynamical memory units with input-dependent leak rates to encode sequences.
A decoder attends to memory outputs rather than the full token history; recurrence supports O(T) work and O(log T) parallel depth.
Matches Transformer closely in language modeling, outperforms both baselines on several cognitive tasks, and remains behind Mamba on language modeling.
Shows stronger selective-copy length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer; performance has task-dependent limitations.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
authors: Cheng Liang, Tengfei Zhang, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped models can improve reasoning through shared-weight repeated computation, but normally require more training FLOPs.
UpLoop starts with a shallow Transformer, copies learned layers to grow depth, and later repeats a shared middle block.
It exactly matches a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, training tokens, and total training FLOPs.
Across model scales, it improves language modeling and downstream performance; at 1.3B parameters, the 22-task average rises from 22.99 to 27.52.
Benefits also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.
authors: Ziteng Wang, Jianqiao Lu, Xinyu Ma, Jintao Zhang, Jun Zhu, Yiyuan Ma, Jianfei Chen
bullets: Problem: Standard residuals force the state width carried through depth to match each layer’s compute width.
Method: Group layers into blocks with d-dimensional PreNorm layers and a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual, linked by learned projections.
Contribution: Makes residual width an independent scaling variable using only dense projections and normalizations.
Results: Reports 1.30× better FLOPs efficiency, 0.0208 lower training loss, and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy in the stated experiments.
Scope: Designed to reduce activation memory and I/O relative to other residual-expansion methods without specialized kernels or infrastructure changes.

papers.title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
papers.tldr: HiRes decouples residual width from per-layer compute width, improving scaling efficiency with a simple Transformer modification.

papers.abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.
authors: Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv, Zhou Lv
bullets: Addresses the tension between local neighbor graphs that miss long-range interactions and quadratic-cost all-pair attention.
Maps centroid-relative atomic distances to learned radial features and combines them with content-dependent queries and keys.
Uses factorized aggregation and readout for linear scaling with atom count at fixed feature dimensions.
Inserted between EquiformerV3 local blocks, with conservative forces obtained by differentiating the energy.
On OPoly26 polymer-derived clusters, matched 5M models reduce per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%; the 20M model achieves 15.81 meV total-energy MAE and 2.619 meV/angstrom force MAE.

Each node reads the shared statistics through its radial features and query, and receives a scalar residual update. The basis curves are schematic, rather than fitted checkpoint values.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in force fields, achieving linear complexity in atom count through factorized aggregation.
papers.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
papers.tldr: Radial Kernel Attention adds a linear-cost global communication pathway that substantially improves energy and force prediction for polymer machine-learning force fields.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.tldr: A dual-budget framework analyzes sparse diffusion models by separately constraining attention connectivity and expert activation, with reported gains through 16K tokens but degradation at longer lengths and a 20% cost reduction under an unspecified timing convention.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware sparse linear attention with recurrent-event selection improves long-context prefill computation and memory traffic.
papers.title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention

papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: We present FloodDiffusion 2 (FD2), an efficient and controllable framework that builds upon FloodDiffusion (FD1), a state-of-the-art streaming motion generation model. While FD1 produces plausible motion, it suffers from low efficiency and limited controllability, as its attention design requires repeated computation over the entire history, and it lacks precise trajectory control for real-world applications. To address these limitations and improve generation quality, FD2 introduces three advances. First, Partial Attention makes finalized history representations independent of the active window, enabling KV-cached inference and shared-history packing for efficient training. Second, we establish a necessary-and-sufficient Bregman criterion for regression losses to preserve diffusion's conditional-mean velocity field. This criterion guides an FK-induced quadratic loss that incorporates motion geometry without online FK evaluation. Third, FD2 introduces precise path conditioning to control the character's root trajectory while preserving natural body motion. Experiments show that FD2 reduces training computation by 4.6$\times$ and accelerates denoising by 11.29$\times$, reaching 2.303 ms per update on long sequences. Alongside these efficiency gains, FD2 improves motion quality over FD1 and achieves state-of-the-art FID scores among streaming methods, with 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
bullets: Targets FD1’s repeated-history computation and limited trajectory control.
Uses Partial Attention for KV-cached inference and shared-history packing during training.
Introduces a Bregman-based criterion and FK-induced quadratic loss to incorporate motion geometry without online forward-kinematics evaluation.
Adds precise root-path conditioning while preserving natural full-body motion.
Reports 4.6× lower training computation, 11.29× faster denoising, and improved FID over FD1, including 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
